title: Materials and their applications

book.title: My Revision Notes: AQA A Level Design and Technology: Product Design

needs: Define mechanical properties and physical properties.
Name and define the five kinds of strength.
Define hardness, toughness, plasticity, ductility, malleability and elasticity.
Define the physical, electrical, thermal and optical properties.
Justify a material choice by linking a property to what the product does.

doNow.q: Which property lets a material be drawn out into a wire?
Besides its properties, name two things that affect material choice.
doNow.a: Any two: aesthetics, cost, manufacturing method, disposal and reuse.

doNow.q: What does a thermal insulator do?
doNow.a: It stops heat passing through the material.

doNow.q: How is a translucent material different from a transparent one?
doNow.a: Translucent diffuses the light so things look blurred; transparent lets you see clearly through.

clues: I let a material be drawn out under tension without cracking.
Without me, you couldn't stretch metal into a wire.

chunks.label: Choosing materials
chunks.summary: Pick a material for the properties the product needs, then justify it.

items.text: Choice balances aesthetics, cost, manufacturing method, disposal and reuse.
The final choice rests mostly on product function and material properties.
Name the exact property and link it to the product, never just 'strong'.

check.q: What mostly decides the final choice of material?
check.a: What the product has to do (its function) and the material's properties.

check.q: Why is 'it's strong' a weak reason for choosing a material?
check.a: It's too general: name the exact property and say why the product needs it.

chunks.label: Mechanical: strength
chunks.summary: Resisting the different kinds of force that act on a material.

items.text: How a material reacts when an external force acts on it.
Withstands being crushed or shortened by pushing forces (compression).
Resists being stretched by pulling forces (tension).
Resists forces that would bend the material.
Resists sliding forces acting along a parallel plane.
Withstands twisting forces from applied torque (torsion).

chunks.label: Other mechanical properties
chunks.summary: How a material copes with wear, impact and being reshaped.

items.text: Resists abrasive wear such as scratching, indentation or cutting.
Absorbs an impact force without fracturing.
Can be permanently deformed and keeps its new shape.
Can be drawn out thinner under tension without cracking, as in wire.
Can be deformed by compression without cracking; easier when hotter.
Can be deformed, then returns to its original shape when the force goes.

check.a: The ability to absorb an impact force without fracturing.

check.q: How is elasticity different from plasticity?
check.a: An elastic material returns to its original shape; a plastic one keeps its new shape.

chunks.label: Physical properties
chunks.summary: Properties that come from what the material is made of.

items.text: Linked to the material's actual make-up or structure.
The mass of the material in a standard volume.
Can be melted from solid to liquid by heat, vital for casting metal.
A natural force that makes the material attract iron or steels.
Withstands attack and decay from the environment.

check.q: Why does a metal for casting need good fusibility?
check.a: It has to be turned from a solid into a liquid by heat so it can be cast.
The mass of the material in a standard volume.

chunks.label: Electrical and thermal
chunks.summary: How electricity and heat pass through a material.

items.text: Lets electric current flow through with very little resistance.
Stops electricity flowing through the material.
Lets heat pass through it, quickly if its conductivity is high.
Stops heat passing through the material.
The material's volume increases when it is heated.

check.q: What does a good electrical conductor give to the flow of charge?

check.a: The material's volume increasing in response to heat.

chunks.label: Optical properties
chunks.summary: How much light a material lets through.

items.text: Lets no light travel through.
Lets light through but diffuses it so objects look blurred; frosted glass is one.
Lets light pass easily, so you can see clearly through it.

check.q: Is frosted glass opaque, translucent or transparent?
What can you do through a transparent material?

apply.q: A plastic toy for toddlers will often be dropped on hard floors and must not crack.
reasons: It absorbs an impact force without fracturing
It can be drawn out into a wire
It can be shaped by compression without cracking
It keeps a new shape after being deformed

apply.q: A bathroom window must let daylight in but stop people seeing in clearly.
reasons: It lets light through but diffuses it, so objects look blurred
It lets you see clearly through it
It stops all light travelling through
It lets heat pass through quickly

apply.q: The outer covering of a mains cable must stop current reaching the user's hand.
reasons: It does not allow electricity to flow through it
It gives very little resistance to the flow of charge
Its volume increases when it is heated

oddOne.q: Which is the odd one out?

items.why: The only mechanical property: the rest are physical properties.
The only one that is a measure (mass in a standard volume).
The only one about changing state, from solid to liquid.
The only one that is a force attracting iron or steels.

options: How a material reacts to an external force
quiz.why: Mechanical properties describe how a material reacts when a force acts on it.

quiz.q: The final choice of material depends mostly on its cost.
quiz.why: Cost is part of the compromise, but function and the material's properties matter most.

quiz.q: 'It's strong' fully justifies the choice of a material.
quiz.why: Name the exact property, such as tensile strength, and link it to what the product does.
Pulling forces put a material in tension, which tensile strength resists.

quiz.q: A screwdriver shaft is twisted hard as a screw is driven in. Which strength does it need?
quiz.why: Twisting forces from torque are resisted by torsional strength.

quiz.q: Shear strength is the ability to resist sliding forces along a parallel plane.
quiz.why: Shear forces slide one part of the material past another.

quiz.q: Which property lets a material absorb an impact without fracturing?
quiz.why: Toughness is about absorbing impact force; hardness is about resisting wear.

quiz.q: Malleability increases as the temperature rises.
quiz.why: A hotter material can be deformed by compression more easily without cracking.

quiz.q: What is the difference between plasticity and elasticity?
options: Plastic deformation is permanent; elastic deformation recovers
Elastic deformation is permanent; plastic deformation recovers
Both are permanent changes of shape
Neither involves a change of shape
quiz.why: A plastic material keeps its new shape; an elastic one returns to its original shape.

quiz.q: Which property is essential for a metal that is going to be cast?
quiz.why: Casting needs a metal that heat can turn into a liquid.

quiz.q: Density is the mass of a material in a standard volume.
quiz.why: Density compares mass with a fixed volume of the material.
Magnetism is the natural force that attracts iron or steels.

options: very little resistance to the flow of charge
a lot of resistance to the flow of charge
quiz.why: Current flows easily through a good conductor.

quiz.q: Thermal expansion means a material's volume gets smaller when it is heated.
Frosted glass is an example of which kind of material?
quiz.why: It lets light through but diffuses it, so objects look blurred.

quiz.q: An opaque material lets light travel through it.
quiz.why: Opaque materials stop light travelling through.

written.q: A designer is choosing a material for a kitchen worktop. Explain why the material needs hardness and toughness.
points: Hardness: it resists abrasive wear such as scratching, indentation or cutting…
…so knives and pans don't scratch or dent the worktop.
Toughness: it absorbs an impact force without fracturing…
…so a heavy pan dropped on it won't crack it.
written.model: Hardness means the worktop resists abrasive wear such as scratching, indentation or cutting, so knives and pans don't scratch or dent it. Toughness means it absorbs an impact force without fracturing, so a heavy pan dropped on it won't crack it.
written.note: For each property: 1 mark for what it is, 1 for linking it to the worktop.

points: The ability to be drawn out (stretched) under tension…
…reducing the cross-sectional area without cracking, for example into a wire.
written.model: Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn out under tension, reducing its cross-sectional area without cracking, for example into a wire.

points: Both describe how a material behaves when a force deforms it.
Plasticity: the deformation is permanent.
A plastic material keeps (retains) its deformed shape.
Elasticity: the material returns to its original shape when the force is removed.
An elastic material only returns if its elastic limit has not been exceeded.
written.model: Both describe how a material behaves when a force deforms it. With plasticity the deformation is permanent and the material keeps its deformed shape, but with elasticity the material returns to its original shape when the force is removed, as long as its elastic limit has not been exceeded.
written.note: 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. At least one point on each property.

written.q: Explain why a saucepan uses a thermal conductor for its base and a thermal insulator for its handle.
points: The base is a thermal conductor, so it lets heat energy transfer through it…
…quickly, to heat the food (high thermal conductivity).
The handle is a thermal insulator, so it stops heat transferring through it…
…so the handle stays safe to hold.
written.model: The base is a thermal conductor, so heat energy transfers through it quickly to heat the food. The handle is a thermal insulator, which stops heat transferring through it, so it stays safe to hold.
written.note: 1 mark per point, up to 3. At least one point on each part.

written.q: Apart from its properties, describe the factors a designer weighs up when selecting a material.
points: Aesthetics: how it looks and feels, such as colour, texture and surface finish.
Cost: such as the raw material price, waste, tooling and finishing.
Manufacturing method: such as the stock forms available and how it can be formed and joined.
Disposal and reuse: such as how easily it can be reused or recycled at the end of its life.
written.model: The designer weighs up aesthetics, such as the colour, texture and surface finish; cost, such as the raw material price, waste, tooling and finishing; the manufacturing method, such as the stock forms available and how it can be formed and joined; and disposal and reuse, such as how easily it can be reused or recycled at the end of its life.
written.note: 1 mark per factor described, up to 4.

written.q: Explain why good fusibility is essential for a metal that is going to be cast.
points: Fusibility is the ability to be turned from a solid into a liquid (molten) state by heat…
…and casting needs the metal molten so it can be cast into shape.
written.model: Fusibility is the ability to be turned from a solid into a molten state by heat, and the metal must be molten so it can be cast into shape.
written.note: 1 mark for the point, 1 for explaining it.
